newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Rebel leader arrives in Zaire's diamond capital.
newsitem.headline: Rebel leader arrives in Zaire's diamond capital.

text.p: Rebel leader Laurent Kabila arrived in victory in Zaire's diamond capital on Monday to a smaller popular welcome but with the prospect of mining wealth to finance his war against President Mobutu Sese Seko.
Hundreds of residents turned out at Mbuji-Mayi airport to greet Kabila who flew in from the eastern city of Goma. Hundreds on the streets shouted support as he drove into the city.
The central region of Kasai, with its capital Mbuji-Mayi, is the homeland of veteran opposition leader Etienne Tshisekedi, who last week offered ministry posts to rebels but was rebuffed.
About 2,000 people who had gathered at Mbuji-Mayi airport left before Kabila arrived with a heavy escort of bodyguards.
The turnout was smaller than the thousands who met him on his first visit to the northeastern capital of Kisangani, the centre for a failed government counter-offensive in January.

"Kisangani was a psychological victory because it was believed that would be our Waterloo. It was the beginning of a certain confidence in our war," said rebel justice commissioner Mwenze Kongolo. "Mbuji-Mayi is not such a big pyschological victory but it is still important in money terms because we have deprived Mobutu of his power to fight us."
Kabila was widely expected to sign new mining contracts with companies in Mbuji-Mayi. A mining official said looters had left diamond stores untouched at the country's only modern mines.

"There was pillage at the mines. We haven't done an inventory so don't know how much but they didn't break into the diamond storehouses," Mfwamba Tchobobo, director of Miniere de Bakwanga (MIBA), told Reuters.
MIBA are Zaire's only modern mines and officially produce diamonds worth about $80 million annually. MIBA dominates the local economy and is Zaire's biggest foreign exchange earner.
Kasai uses different banknotes to defy Mobutu and is a crucial test of support for the AFDL, which has seized more than a third of Africa's third largest country since October.
Residents raised a banner outside the house where Kabila was staying in Mbuji-Mayi in support of Tshisekedi and his party.
Local officials of Tshisekedi's UPDS party later arrived at the house to greet Kabila but were turned away by his guards.
"We support Kabila and Tshisekedi. They are both against Mobutu and though there is some difference between them now they can sort it out," said UPDS director for east Kasai Kabongo Mukunde.
Tshisekedi's Baluba people in Kasai in 1993 heeded his call to boycott new bank notes introduced by Mobutu.
Kabila's origins also lie with the Baluba, but in a subgroup from neighbouring mineral-rich Shaba. Hundreds of thousands of Kasaians were expelled from Shaba province in the early 1990s.

Residents said government troops fled the city on Friday after looting and the first rebels of Kabila's Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (AFDL) had arrived the same day and were reinforced on Saturday.

"There was no fighting in the city. On Saturday, people came and welcomed the liberators and carried their weapons," said Tshikala Ndaie, a priest and vicar-general of the Liberal Catholic Church of Congo.
Residents said civilians looted Zairean government buildings including the headquarters of the civil guard. One man said 20 people had been killed, some in fighting between rival troops.
They said the soldiers had fled in looted vehicles with up to 3,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees including former Rwandan troops towards Kananga city, 140 km (90 miles) west of Mbuji-Mayi.
Church sources said on Monday Zairean troops looted Kananga on Sunday night and it was expected to fall to the rebels.
